blocks.text: Stationary waves can be set up in other media also, such as air column inside a pipe or tube. A common example of vibrating air column is in the organ pipe.
Organ pipe

An organ pipe is a wind instrument in which sound is produced, due to setting up of stationary waves in air column. It consists of a hollow long tube with both ends open or with one end open and the other closed. The relationship between the incident wave and the reflected wave depends upon whether the reflecting end of the pipe is open or closed.

items: (i) If the reflecting end is open, the air molecules have complete freedom of motion and this behaves as an antinode.
(ii) If the reflecting end is closed, then it behaves as a node because the movement of the molecules is restricted.

blocks.text: Modes of Vibrations
Stationary longitudinal waves occur in a pipe as discussed by the following two cases:
Case (1): Modes of vibrations in an organ pipe open at both ends

Let us consider an organ pipe of length l which is open at both ends. As at the open end, an air molecule has complete freedom of motion so it acts as antinode as shown in Fig. 7.8. In this figure, longitudinal waves set up inside the pipe have been represented by transverse curved lines which represent the displacement and amplitude of vibration of air particles at various points along the axis of pipe.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: f₃ = 3f₁ is the third harmonic, since the harmonic number is f/f₁ = 3. It is the second mode of vibration of a pipe closed at one end, which has only odd harmonics (as the caption of Fig. 7.9 says).

blocks.title: A Scientific Fact
blocks.text: In an organ pipe, the primary driving mechanism is wavering, sheet like jet of air from flute-slit, which interacts with the upper lip and the air column in the pipe to maintain a steady oscillation.

blocks.alt: A vertical organ pipe (orange walls, yellow inside) on a tapered foot. Air (arrow at the bottom) rises through the foot, flows along the curved face of a dark block and leaves through the narrow flue-slit at the mouth on the left. Above the mouth the sheet-like jet wavers about the upper lip, curling into eddies alternately outside and inside the pipe; a small arrow at the top left points upward.
blocks.caption: A Scientific Fact (PDF page 153): the wavering, sheet-like air jet from the flue-slit of an organ pipe (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.title: Example 7.4
blocks.problem:
An organ pipe has a length of 50 cm. Find the frequency of its fundamental note and the next harmonic, when it is:
(a) open at both ends
(b) closed at one end
(speed of sound = 350 m s⁻¹)
steps:
a) When pipe is open at both ends:
Fundamental frequency   f₁ = ?
Next harmonic frequency   f₂ = ?

The frequency for nth harmonic in an open organ pipe is:
fₙ = n (v/2l)   when n = 1, 2, 3, ………

so the fundamental frequency is,
f₁ = (1 × 350)/(2 × 0.5)   put n = 1
f₁ = 350 Hz

Next harmonic frequency i.e., n = 2 is:
f₂ = 2v/2l
f₂ = v/l = 350/0.5
f₂ = 700 Hz

b) When pipe is closed at one end:
Fundamental frequency   f₁ = ?
Next harmonic frequency   f₃ = ?

When the pipe is closed at one end then frequency for nth harmonic is:
fₙ = n (v/4l)   when n = 1, 3, 5, 7, ………

So fundamental frequency is:
f₁ = (1 × 350)/(4 × 0.5)   put n = 1
f₁ = 175 Hz

Next harmonic frequency i.e., n = 3 is:
f₃ = 3v/4l
f₃ = (3 × 350)/(4 × 0.5)

blocks.title: Ponder Upon
blocks.text: Open pipes produce all harmonics, while closed pipes produced only odd harmonics.

blocks.title: Example 7.5
blocks.problem: A church organ consists of pipes, each open at one end, of different lengths. The minimum length is 30 mm and the longest is 4 m. Calculate the frequency range of the fundamental notes. (speed of sound = 340 m s⁻¹)
steps:
l_min = 30 mm = (30/1000) m = 30 × 10⁻³ m
l_max = 4 m
v = 340 m s⁻¹
Frequency range = ?

For an organ pipe open at one end only:
fₙ = nv/4l

(i) Minimum length
For fundamental frequency, put n = 1
f₁,max = nv/4l_min
f₁,max = (1 × 340)/(4 × 30 × 10⁻³)
f₁,max = 2833.33 Hz

(ii) Maximum length:
For fundamental frequency, put n = 1
f₁,min = nv/4l_max
f₁,min = (1 × 340)/(4 × 4)
f₁,min = 21.25 Hz
blocks.answer: So, the fundamental frequency range is approximately from 21 Hz to 2833 Hz.
